full_judgment:
8. Mr AB Siddique, learned Advocate for the petitioner, took us through section 14 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 and Articles 158 and 178 of the Limitation Act and submitted that the petitioner was entitled to file objection within a period of [90+30=] 120 days and the petitioner filed his objection on 24-9-2001 well within the time, but the learned Joint District Judge most illegally found the objection barred by limitation. 

 10. On the other hand, Mr Mohiuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party No.1, took us through the record. "In the written objection, the petitioner stated that the petitioner received on 3-11-2000 the notice dated 23-1-2000 of the making of the award: After filing of the award in Court on 9-5-2001, the petitioner appeared on 26-6-2001 and obtained time to file objection to the award. By such step, the petitioner was well aware of filing of the award in Court. In view of Article 158 of the Limitation Act, Mr Mohiuddin Ahmed submitted that the objection filed on 24-9-2001 was hopelessly barred by limitation and learned Judge did not commit any error in rejecting such belated objection. 

 12. Only issue facing us is, whether or not the objection filed by the petitioner on 24-9-2001 was barred by limitation. 

 14. Article 178 of the Limitation Act gives 90 days from the date of service of notice of the making of the award for filing of the award in Court. The notice was served on the petitioner on 3-11-2000. But the umpire did not file the award in Court within said period of 90 days from service of the notice. The umpire however filed his award on 9-5-2001. It is true that after filing of the award, the Court was required to issue a notice of such filing of the award in Court but it did not issue any notice. 

 15. Article 158 of the Limitation Act gives a period of 30 days from the date of service of notice of filing of the award in Court to take step for either setting aside the a-vard or to get the award remitted for reconsideration. 

 16. After the petitioner having appeared in Court and taken time for more than three occasions, specifically to file objection against the award filed, failure of the Court in issuing the statuary notice under section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act would neither extend the period of limitation nor entitle the petitioner to file objection beyond said period of 30 days. Such steps on behalf of the petitioner are sufficient not only to fix the petitioner with the notice of filing of the award in Court but also to dispense with the requirement of issue of the notice by the Court. 

 18. Such failure on the part of the umpire is no doubt an irregularity but such irregularity per se would neither invalidate the award nor extend the period of limitation entitling the petitioner to file his objection against the award beyond thirty days; cf Dhaka Leather Complex vs Sikder Construction Limited, 55 DLR 578. 

 19. In the circumstances, we find no reason to take a view different from that of the learned Joint District Judge that the objection against the award as was filed by the petitioner was barred by limitation. The learned Judge therefore committed no error in rejecting the objection of the petitioner against the award. Nor such decision has resulted in any failure of justice.
